To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV infection remodels T cell immunometabolism, with the viral accessory proteins Nef and Vpu antagonizing amino acid transport.

HIV infection of T cells causes a massive remodeling of the T cell surface that includes downregulation of many proteins, including the amino acid transporters SNAT1 and SERINC3/4; and Vpu antagonism of SNAT1 and Nef antagonism of SERINC3/3/4 are required for efficient HIV replication.

HIV infection of T cells downregulates the amino acid transporter Solute Carrier Family 38 Member 1 (SLC38A1, SNAT1), and that this downregulation is antagonized by the HIV accessory proteins Vpu and NEF.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of host cell proteins that are targeted by the HIV accessory proteins Vpu and Nif during infection.
the mechanisms by which viruses such as HIV evade the immune system and cause disease.
the molecular mechanisms that govern the interactions of HIV-1 and the host immune system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proteomics study of HIV infection in CD4+ T-cells revealed the antagonism of amino acid metabolism by Vpu and by Nef.

the proteomic analysis of HIV-infected cells revealed the downregulation of a large set of plasma membrane proteins that are involved in a wide range of cellular functions, including amino acid metabolism.
this study provides an unbiased and quantitative proteomics approach to identify host cell surface proteins downregulated during HIV-1 infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have taken a quantitative proteomic approach to identify cell surface proteins that are downregulated during HIV-1 infection of CD4 T cells and that we have focused on one of these proteins, SNAT1, which is a transporter that transports the amino acid alanine.
we have identified a number of proteins that are downregulated during HIV-1 infection, and have identified the mechanisms by which this occurs.
HIV infection remodels T cell surface immunoreceptor composition, and this is accomplished by the virus through antagonism of host amino acid metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HIV Vpu protein antagonizes the amino acid transporter system N system to promote viral replication.
the proteome-wide, quantitative approach used in this study can be used to identify novel, unanticipated host cell factors that are down-regulated or otherwise affected by viral infection.
the proteomic approach that we have taken has allowed us to uncover a new mechanism by which the virus can interfere with host cell function, namely by interfering with amino acid metabolism.
